h1: NMC Advertising Guidelines 2026: What Doctors, Clinics and Hospitals Can (and Can't) Do Online
quickAnswer:
On 6 October 2026, the National Medical Commission issued guidelines on ethical advertising that took effect immediately. Doctors cannot self-promote, solicit patients, use testimonials, before-and-after photos, "best" or "No.1" claims, or AI-generated promotional campaigns. Hospitals may share factual, verifiable information. Agencies and influencers acting for a doctor do not shift the responsibility.

This article explains the guidelines for marketing planning and is not legal advice.

blocks.text: The Ethics and Medical Registration Board of the NMC released the "Guidelines on Ethical Advertising and Public Communication" through a public notice dated 6 October 2026, effective immediately. They were framed in light of a Supreme Court writ petition and the Indian Medical Council (Professional Conduct, Etiquette and Ethics) Regulations, 2002 (Medical Dialogues; full guidelines PDF).

Advertising is defined broadly: any communication that directly or indirectly promotes a doctor's or institution's services, reputation, qualifications or facilities — including content created with AI or published through an agency or influencer (The South First).

sections.heading: What can't doctors and clinics do?

blocks.text: Based on the published guidelines, registered medical practitioners (RMPs) should not:

items: Solicit patients directly or indirectly, or engage third parties to market their services
Use patient testimonials, endorsements, celebrity patients or promotional patient stories
Post before-and-after photos or advertise surgical results, except anonymised scientific or educational material
Claim "best", "No.1", "leading", "100% success", "guaranteed cure", "painless" or similar, unless independently verifiable
Run fear-based marketing or create demand for unnecessary tests or procedures
Use discounts, coupons, free procedures, contests or referral rewards that encourage unnecessary care
Buy followers, likes, reviews or ratings, or manipulate search rankings
Endorse drugs, devices or health products
Run AI-generated promotional campaigns for commercial gain, or use AI to create fake patients, testimonials or outcomes

blocks.text: Patient consent alone does not make an otherwise prohibited testimonial or before-and-after post acceptable.
The guidelines do not ban doctors from social media. Permitted activity includes:

items: Public health education, awareness talks and academic content that doesn't promote a personal practice
Formal announcements: starting a practice, changing address or type of practice, temporary absence, resumption, and declaring fees
Health information leaflets for patients visiting the clinic, without cure guarantees or superiority claims
Greetings on national or medical-profession days without promotional content
Research-based case studies published in reputed medical journals

blocks.text: When doctors publish on electronic media, they must disclose their name, qualifications, registration status and State or National Medical Register number.

sections.heading: What can hospitals and medical institutions advertise?

blocks.text: Hospitals may share factual, objective and verifiable information: name, location, contact details, departments, facilities, equipment, emergency services, accreditation and charges. They may not include patient solicitation, inducements, superiority claims, cure guarantees or promotional portrayal of an individual doctor. A website directory listing doctors' names, qualifications, specialties, registration details and availability is treated as patient information, not advertising. Hospitals are also governed by the applicable Clinical Establishments Act or state law.

sections.heading: What does this mean for digital marketing agencies?

blocks.text: Two provisions matter directly. First, using an agency, influencer or platform does not absolve the doctor or hospital of responsibility for content they authorise. Second, agency payments must not be structured so that payment is linked to procuring or referring individual patients — which affects pay-per-patient or pay-per-appointment models for doctors. Clinics should review agency contracts now.

State Medical Councils can take graded action against doctors after a show-cause notice: a warning and ethics training for a first violation, censure and a monetary penalty for a second, and suspension of registration for repeated or serious violations, up to removal from the register for one to three years. Doctors can appeal to the NMC's Ethics and Medical Registration Board within 60 days.

sections.heading: A compliant marketing plan for clinics and hospitals

items: Audit existing content. Remove testimonials, before-and-after posts, superiority claims and inducement offers from Instagram, YouTube, Google Business Profile and your website.
Add disclosures. Include doctors' qualifications and registration numbers on posts and profile pages.
Lead with education. Build content around conditions, prevention and what to expect — the kind of material patients and AI search both value.
Strengthen factual visibility. Keep Google Business Profile, departments, timings, facilities and fees accurate and complete. Local SEO is factual information, not solicitation.
Handle reviews ethically. Never buy or manipulate reviews; respond to existing ones professionally without sharing patient details.
Label AI-assisted content where its artificial nature matters, and never use AI to create patient likenesses or outcomes.
Review agency contracts so fees are not tied to individual patient referrals.
Get legal sign-off for campaigns where you are unsure.

faqs.question: Can doctors still use Instagram in India?
faqs.answer: Yes, for public health education and factual information, with name, qualifications and registration number disclosed. Self-promotion, testimonials and patient solicitation are not permitted.

faqs.question: Can hospitals run Google or Meta ads?
faqs.answer: The guidelines allow hospitals to disseminate factual, verifiable institutional information and leave the detail to state clinical establishment laws. Ads that solicit patients, offer inducements or make superiority claims are not permitted. Check with your legal adviser before running campaigns.

faqs.question: Are Google reviews allowed?
faqs.answer: Reviews that patients leave on their own are not prohibited, but doctors and hospitals must not procure, manipulate or buy reviews, or use them as promotional testimonials.

faqs.question: Do the guidelines apply to AI-generated content?
faqs.answer: Yes. AI-generated promotional campaigns for commercial gain are prohibited, and permitted AI content must be marked as AI-generated.

faqs.question: When did the guidelines take effect?
faqs.answer: Immediately, from the public notice dated 6 October 2026.
